strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance: heterogeneous advantage distributions in multitask RL are convincingly demonstrated and address a real limitation in methods like GRPO
Technically sound approach with correct mathematical derivations: modulation factors maintaining geometric mean of 1 properly ensures balanced scaling without unintended step-size changes

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: systematic assessment across 10 behavioral tasks with proper baselines (GRPO, RLOO, GPG, RE++), thorough ablations isolating each component, and zero-shot generalization analysis

Strong and consistent empirical results: best average task rank of 1.20, up to +42.29% improvement over GRPO on difficult tasks, particularly strong on pragmatic tasks requiring reasoning (humor/sarcasm detection)
Thoughtful component-wise design: three-part mechanism (contribution signals, geometric centering, inertial smoothing) is well-justified with good intuition for why each element matters
Good interpretability analysis: qualitative reasoning traces (Figures 2-3) show richer, more contextually grounded reasoning compared to baselines
Reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, dataset descriptions, and commitment to release code
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core contribution: applying geometric mean-based weighting to advantages is relatively incremental over established multitask learning methods (gradient balancing, uncertainty weighting); the paper understates connections to classical multitask optimization literature

Narrow evaluation scope: training limited to specialized Human Behavior Atlas benchmark; all RL comparisons use identical base model; zero-shot generalization tested on only 2 tasks; no evaluation on other multitask RL domains (robotics, games, etc.) limits generalizability claims

Insufficient theoretical justification for contribution signals: using average absolute advantages as proxy for gradient contribution needs stronger derivation from policy gradient theorem; why absolute values vs. positive advantages only is unexplained
Hyperparameters lack principled justification: βρ=βs=0.95 and reward weights (wfmt=0.2, λlen=0.75) chosen without sensitivity analysis; no guidance on how to set these for new domains
Inconsistent benefits across tasks: sample-level modulation provides no improvement for EMO, INT, SOC; paper fails to characterize when/why HARPO helps vs. hurts, limiting applicability guidance
Missing computational cost analysis: no comparison of training time, memory, or computational overhead versus GRPO despite adding contribution signal tracking and smoothing operations

Qualitative reasoning assessment: reasoning quality improvements rely on manual inspection; LLM-Judge evaluation introduces potential biases; claims about 'more explicit reasoning' lack quantitative metrics

Incomplete comparison with multitask learning literature: no direct adaptation/comparison with gradient balancing methods (GradNorm, uncertainty weighting), curriculum learning, or meta-learning approaches in RL settings

Overstated generalization claims: only 2 held-out tasks evaluated; connection between balanced training and transfer is correlational not causal; 'more transferable features' inference needs stronger evidence
Limited characterization of problem scope: evaluation confined to behavioral/affective computing; unclear if HARPO addresses genuine heterogeneity issues or simply fits this specialized domain well

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies how heterogeneous behavioral data causes uneven learning in multitask settings
Clear and thorough methodology: geometric mean centering and inertial smoothing are well-justified design choices with careful mathematical development
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 10 behavioral tasks, ablations on all components, zero-shot generalization tests, and extensive supplementary results
Strong results within scope: achieves best average task rank (1.20), more balanced learning than baselines, improved generalization on AUT/SER tasks
Excellent presentation: well-written with effective figures and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combining existing multitask learning techniques (advantage modulation, geometric normalization, exponential smoothing) is incremental; lacks theoretical justification or convergence analysis

Suspicious empirical results: GRPO's catastrophic failure on SAR (27.56% vs 69.85%) is unexplained and suggests implementation issues or hyperparameter misalignment, undermining confidence in all comparisons
Narrow evaluation scope: only tested on one benchmark (Human Behavior Atlas), one base model (Qwen 2.5-Omni-7B), and one domain (social behavior); no evidence of generalization
Insufficient ablation studies: no exploration of arithmetic mean as alternative to geometric mean; no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for βρ, βs; no comparison with alternative modulation schemes
Unjustified design choices: using advantage magnitudes as contribution signals is intuitive but unvalidated; no comparison with gradient norms, loss reduction, or other measures
Weak reasoning analysis: largely qualitative with cherry-picked examples (Figures 2-3); claims about explicit reasoning are anecdotal without quantitative metrics
No statistical testing: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; lack of inter-judge agreement for LLM-based evaluation metrics
Missing theoretical insight: no formal problem characterization, convergence guarantees, or analysis of when/why the method should work vs. fail
Unclear hyperparameter tuning: while claiming fair comparison, no evidence of equal tuning effort across methods; baseline hyperparameters taken from original papers may disadvantage some methods

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates limitations of task-specific models and existing multitask approaches without heterogeneity awareness
Principled technical design: geometric mean reference ensures modulation factors maintain mean 1; two-level modulation (sample and task) addresses heterogeneity systematically
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 10 diverse behavioral tasks, multiple RL baselines (GRPO/RLOO/GPG/RE++), systematic ablations, qualitative reasoning analysis
Strong empirical results: best average rank (1.20), substantial improvements on weak tasks (SAR +17%, HUM +42%), consistent across methods
Reproducibility and transparency: detailed hyperparameters, complete reward design specifications, algorithm pseudocode, promise of code release
Insightful empirical analysis: Figure 4 directly links advantage modulation to weak-task learning, advantage distributions justify approach, modulation factor dynamics examined
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is GRPO with geometric-mean advantage modulation; advantage reweighting and multitask balancing are well-established (Kendall et al. 2018, Yu et al. 2020)
Single-domain evaluation: experiments only on Human Behavior Atlas benchmark; unclear if HARPO generalizes to other multitask RL domains (robotics, vision, non-social NLP)

Experimental concerns: LLM-judge evaluation for 3/10 tasks introduces brittleness; some baselines show suspiciously poor performance (GRPO HUM: 27.56%, RE++ INT: 5.01%) suggesting implementation/tuning issues; no confidence intervals or multiple runs
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: βρ=0.95, βs=0.95 appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; missing comparison to simpler baselines (uniform weighting, inverse variance)
Generalization validation incomplete: held-out evaluation on only 2 tasks within same domain; modest improvement on AUT (+2%); no out-of-domain generalization demonstrated

Reward design not thoroughly ablated: multiple components (task accuracy, format, length) combined with fixed weights; no ablation on these design choices or sensitivity analysis; weights appear domain-specific
Modest ablation effect sizes: sample-level modulation rank change 2.60→1.90 is small; structured modulation 2.00→1.90 very small; raises questions about component necessity
Reasoning quality analysis primarily qualitative: Figures 2-3 show few cherry-picked examples; reasoning length statistics only in Figure 1; no automated metrics for reasoning quality
Missing related work comparisons: no evaluation against other multitask optimization methods (gradient surgery, task normalization, uncertainty weighting for reasoning RL)
No computational overhead analysis: training time or memory costs compared to GRPO not reported

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine challenges in heterogeneous multitask behavioral learning with clear empirical evidence of the issue

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across multitask learning (10 tasks), zero-shot generalization (5 held-out tasks), and interpretability analysis with both automated metrics and human evaluation

Solid technical execution with well-justified design choices (e.g., geometric mean-centered modulation proven to have geometric mean of 1) and convincing ablations demonstrating each component contributes meaningfully

Strong empirical results: +12.02% improvement on multitask learning, +9.37% on zero-shot generalization, best performance on all five held-out tasks, and improved reasoning trace consistency (87.7% vs. 66.5%)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed appendix covering algorithms, hyperparameters, reward design, datasets, and promise of code/model release; extensive experimental setup documentation
Clear presentation with logical flow from motivation through technical approach to comprehensive experiments, supported by effective visualizations (Figures 2-7)
weaknesses: Limited theoretical foundation: no convergence analysis, formal fairness characterization, or justification for why advantage magnitude is the right contribution proxy beyond computational convenience; missing theoretical guarantees about balancing mechanism

Incremental technical novelty: core contribution reduces to standard normalization techniques (geometric mean reference + exponential smoothing) applied to GRPO; innovation is primarily engineering-focused rather than conceptual

Hyperparameter choices lack justification: inertial smoothing coefficients (βρ=0.95, βs=0.95) fixed without ablation or sensitivity analysis; reward weights (wfmt=0.2, λlen=0.75) appear arbitrary; no learning rate exploration specific to HARPO

Sample-level modulation shows inconsistent benefits: Table 7 reveals minimal/no improvement for EMO, INT, SOC tasks yet component is retained; paper briefly acknowledges but lacks deeper investigation of why benefits vary and whether complexity is justified

Scope limited to social behavior domain: all experiments confined to Human Behavior Atlas behavioral tasks with no evidence of generalization to other heterogeneous multitask domains (vision, robotics, general reasoning); unclear if insights apply beyond reasoning-based RL

Statistical evaluation gaps: no significance testing (confidence intervals, error bars, p-values), single runs without variance reporting, human evaluation with only 3 annotators and no inter-rater agreement metrics, LLM-judge evaluation without validation of consistency

Ethical concerns underexplored: application to mental health screening (depression, anxiety, PTSD) has serious implications barely discussed; no analysis of dataset fairness across demographics, collection consent, or potential for surveillance/manipulation

Missing analyses: no sensitivity studies on key hyperparameters, incomplete comparison of geometric vs. arithmetic mean references, no deep investigation of failure modes or task-specific challenges explaining low performance on some tasks (NVC: 14.54%)

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation within the behavioral understanding domain: multitask learning on 10 tasks, zero-shot generalization on 5 held-out benchmarks, and detailed reasoning interpretability analysis including human evaluation
Well-motivated problem: correctly identifies that heterogeneous behavioral data with diverse modalities and prediction targets can create imbalanced training signals
Solid empirical execution: careful experimental design with fair comparisons (same base model, reward design, hyperparameters across methods), consistent improvements across most tasks
Good reproducibility materials: extensive appendix with algorithm pseudocode, detailed hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, human annotation protocols, and ablation studies

Interesting interpretability insights: reasoning trace analysis shows improvements in consistency (87.7% vs 66.5%), paraphrase robustness (88.4% vs 80.7%), and token efficiency (19.86 vs 57.69 tokens)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward multiplicative advantage reweighting (A_H = s_(m,q) × s_m × Â). The method simply scales GRPO advantages using geometric mean references—insufficient sophistication for ICML

Weak theoretical justification: paper fails to rigorously justify why absolute advantage magnitude |A| should proxy contribution signals. Using advantage magnitude could introduce bias toward tasks with naturally larger advantages. No formal analysis of convergence or when/why the approach improves multitask learning

Narrow evaluation scope: all experiments limited to Human Behavior Atlas and related behavioral benchmarks. No evaluation on other multitask RL domains (robotics, vision, NLP). Unclear whether HARPO generalizes beyond social behavior processing

Questionable experimental fairness: HARPO was explicitly designed for this benchmark's heterogeneous properties, while baselines (GRPO, RE++) are general-purpose methods. Unfair to show a method outperforms general algorithms on a benchmark it was designed for. Missing comparisons to task-weighting, uncertainty weighting (Kendall et al., 2018), and gradient surgery (Yu et al., 2020) approaches

Modest ablation improvements: w/o structured modulation (rank 2.00 vs 1.90), w/o sample-level modulation (2.60 vs 1.90), w/o inertial control (2.70 vs 1.90)—differences are marginal and components lack clear justification for their necessity

Incomplete statistical analysis: no confidence intervals or significance testing provided. Per-task results show inconsistent wins (many ties with GRPO). Table 1 ranking-based aggregation obscures that HARPO doesn't consistently win on individual tasks

Missing baseline comparisons: no direct comparison to standard multitask learning solutions (task-frequency weighting, uncertainty weighting, curriculum learning). Paper mentions related work but doesn't explain why advantage modulation is superior

Reproducibility gaps: states 'Our model and codes can be found at [no URL]'—critical missing element. Hyperparameter choices (βρ = 0.95, βs = 0.95) lack sensitivity analysis or justification. No ablation on these hyperparameters

Insufficient impact discussion: impact statement essentially declines to address ethical concerns, despite models trained on sensitive behavioral data (depression, anxiety, PTSD detection). Insufficient discussion of potential biases, harms, or limitations for mental health applications

Circular reasoning in contribution signals: if a task naturally produces smaller advantages, it gets upweighted; if it produces larger advantages, it gets downweighted. This could introduce task-type bias rather than fixing true imbalance

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly establishes how heterogeneous behavioral data creates imbalanced learning signals in multitask settings
Principled method design: HARPO combines three well-justified mechanisms (contribution signals, geometric centering, inertial smoothing) with clear intuitions and mathematical soundness
Comprehensive evaluation: spans 10 tasks + 5 held-out benchmarks with multitask (±12%), generalization (±9.37%), and interpretability metrics; thorough ablations isolate component contributions

Strong empirical results: consistent improvements across metrics (best avg. rank 2.10 among RL methods; wins on all zero-shot tasks); particularly effective on challenging pragmatic tasks (SAR +17.06%, HUM +42.29% vs GRPO)

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear writing, Algorithm 1 pseudocode, extensive appendices (hyperparameters, reward design, reasoning evaluation setup), promised code release, fair experimental design with identical base model/data/reward for RL comparisons
Beyond accuracy: focus on reasoning interpretability (consistency, coherence, concision, human eval) with automated+human evaluation is valuable for real-world behavioral applications
Thorough empirical analysis: Figures 2-5 demonstrate mechanism effectiveness; advantage distribution analysis (Fig. 3, 7) provides intuition for why modulation helps
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification: (1) why advantage magnitudes are optimal proxies for gradient contribution (justified only as 'computationally convenient'), (2) why geometric mean specifically vs. arithmetic/median/task-normalized alternatives—missing ablation on reference choice, (3) connection between modulating |Â| and actual policy gradient impact (Eq. 4-5) lacks rigor

Contribution signal design limitations: (1) using absolute advantages ignores sign/direction—tasks with small correct advantages might be unfairly downweighted, (2) no analysis of pathological distributions (near-zero advantages everywhere), (3) limited investigation of signal behavior across training beyond SAR example

Limited experimental scope: (1) all RL methods on identical Qwen 2.5-Omni-7B backbone—generalization to other architectures unclear, (2) no error bars or significance testing despite RL stochasticity, (3) human eval on only 3 annotators without inter-rater agreement, (4) Model comparisons include some trained on more data (marked *), complicating fairness

Modest ablation effects: structured modulation removal shows minimal impact (1.90→2.00 rank), and without statistical testing, effect sizes appear small relative to RL noise; heterogeneous effects across tasks (inertial control SAR +7.96% vs ANX +1.30%) unexplored

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: (1) advantage modulation benefits demonstrated for only SAR; pattern across other weak tasks unclear, (2) no investigation of task properties predicting HARPO effectiveness, (3) limited exploration of when method helps vs. hurts

Hyperparameter exploration: (1) inertial control parameters fixed at βρ, βs=0.95 without reported tuning or sensitivity analysis, (2) reward weights (wfmt=0.2, λlen=0.75) appear fixed without ablation, (3) learning rate reused from GRPO—optimality for modified advantage landscape unexplored

Ethics discussion too brief: behavioral analysis applications (autism detection, depression, PTSD) are clinically sensitive; brief impact statement deferring responsibility insufficient given potential for misuse in surveillance/discrimination

Generalization limitations: zero-shot eval uses behaviorally similar held-out tasks; generalization to entirely different modalities (e.g., video-only→text-only analysis) unexplored; single-task performance under modulation not evaluated
